sections.heading: Strawmap and Roadmap Updates
sections.summary: Native account abstraction is SFI'd for Hegota; Lean SPHINCS is the target PQ transaction signature scheme; Poseidon is being dropped in favor of Blake/SHA.
sections.body:
- Justin Florentine updated the Ethereum strawmap recently; the call reviewed relevant milestones.
- Native account abstraction (moving away from EOAs) is now SFI'd (scheduled) for the Hegota fork.
- A new VM (not tied to execution, consensus, or data-availability layer) is expected to ship by I-Star.
- The post-quantum ECDSA replacement is called Lean SPHINCS, a hash-based signature scheme.
- Three design pillars guide the PQ transaction signature effort:
  - Account abstraction (goodbye to EOAs as currently known)
  - No new cryptographic precompiles — bad experience with BLS precompiles (fought for years to add them, nobody uses them, they now complicate zkVM/snarkification of EVM)
  - Homogeneous hash-based cryptography across consensus, data-availability, and transaction layers
- Poseidon is being dropped as the hash function because Flock (based on Banner Fields) enables fast enough proving of Blake and SHA.
  - Final choice between Blake and SHA is not yet made, but it will not be Poseidon.

sections.heading: SPHINCS Minus Parameter Variants and Hardware Signing Costs
sections.summary: SPHINCS Minus variant C12 targets 2^14 signature budget and only 37,200 hashes for signing, but still takes 47.5 seconds on a Ledger Nano S.
sections.body:
- Antonio used the Riva Labs interactive tool to illustrate SPHINCS parameter trade-offs.
- Standard SLH-DSA-128S (NIST Level 1): ~8 KB signature size, 2^64 signature budget.
- NIST's April 2026 additional parameter set: one large XMSS tree of height 22, targeting 2^24 signatures, reducing size to ~4 KB but requiring 1.45 billion hashes for signing — impractical on hardware wallets (hours or days on a Ledger).
- Nico's SPHINCS Minus C12 variant targets 2^14 signature budget.
  - Justified by mainnet analysis: 99.99% of addresses sent fewer than 3,000 transactions per year in 2025.
  - Optimized for signing cost rather than signature size: only 37,200 hashes needed for signing.
  - Still takes 47.5 seconds on a Ledger Nano S.
- Riva Labs achieved 1.5-second signing on a Ledger Nano S Plus with 2^24 signature budget.
  - Technique combines: computing public parts of SPHINCS outside the secure element, offline precomputation of public values, and grinding during signing.
  - A formal cryptographic analysis paper is planned.
- Key generation benchmarks discussed: Blockstream reported ~14-15 seconds for keygen on Ledger Nano, which Antonio considers acceptable as a one-time setup cost.
- Simon Masson raised that Ledger implementations typically re-derive key material from seed at every power-up/signing step, so keygen time effectively adds to signing time.
  - Post Quantum FBI confirmed Ledger re-derives keys from seed at each power-up; switching profiles requires that time.
  - Antonio and Nico noted that caching intermediate Merkle tree nodes (1 KiB, non-secret) can mitigate this cost.

sections.heading: PQ1 Hardware Wallet by Freedom Factory
sections.summary: Freedom Factory demonstrated a SPHINCS Minus hardware wallet prototype achieving 1.1-second on-silicon signing and 3-second cold-boot signing on an STM32U585.
sections.body:
- Nicola Ceornea (CTO, Freedom Factory) presented the PQ1 (Post-Quantum 1) hardware wallet, an evolution of their Legion1 device.
- Motivated by Google's advances in cracking ECDSA; started prototyping in April 2026 using Nico's SPHINCS Minus (C10 variant).
- Hardware platform: STM32U585 (ARM Cortex-M33) with TrustZone for secure/non-secure world separation.
  - Keys split via XOR between OPTIGA Trust M secure element and NXP SE050 secure element, recombined in the trusted environment for signing.
  - STM32 has a SHA-256 hardware accelerator, which significantly helps performance.
- Achieved ~1.1-second on-silicon signature time and ~3-second cold-boot signature time (including key derivation) with C10.
- Hash function used: SHA-256.
- Also implementing ERC-7730 clear signing.
- Received first EVT (engineering validation test) hardware a few days ago but could not demo due to a proprietary screen connector issue.
- Security approach inspired by Trezor's open-source firmware model.
  - First-stage bootloader hashes firmware on each boot cycle, displays result as eight words for user verification against publicly released values.
  - Devices shipped unprovisioned; users burn fuses/option bytes to lock into production mode.
  - Chip selection based on resistance to known fault-injection attacks.
- All code is open source (work in progress); anyone with the STM32U585 IoT2 evaluation board (~$50, ~$100 with secure elements) can run it today.
- Verification contract uses a modified base smart account (account abstraction, not native EOA).
  - Audit by Trail of Bits is in progress.
  - Exploring formal verification in Lean using Aeneas and Charon tools to translate Rust firmware to Lean, plus EasyCrypt experiments.
  - Also experimenting with AI-generated formal verification code (not audited).
- Target ship date: Q4 2026; near-final hardware revision expected by September 15.
- Plans to attend DEVCON Mumbai and potentially demo devices; applied to speak at OpenHardware events.
- Nico offered a dedicated hardware inspection booth at DEVCON with machines to verify hardware authenticity.

sections.heading: FIPS Compliance for PQ Signatures
sections.summary: FIPS compliance for PQ signatures requires industrial-grade HSMs and is not practical for consumer hardware; secp256k1 was never FIPS-compliant either.
sections.body:
- Manuel Arto asked whether SPHINCS Minus being non-FIPS-compliant could be a problem for institutional smart wallet migration to PQ.
- OKX pointed out that secp256k1 was never FIPS-compliant either.
- Nico confirmed: a FIPS-compliant SPHINCS Minus variant exists in his repo but requires an industrial-grade HSM as the signer.
  - FIPS compliance means using a FIPS-compliant signer; no consumer hardware meets this requirement.
  - Pursuing FIPS compliance is much harder than expected and likely not relevant for regular consumers.

sections.heading: DEVCON Mumbai PQ Showcase Planning
sections.summary: A dedicated post-quantum room at DEVCON Mumbai is being planned for hardware demos and device inspection.
sections.body:
- Antonio mentioned a proposal (possibly from Matteo at Riva Labs) to organize a dedicated post-quantum room at DEVCON Mumbai.
- Freedom Factory plans to attend with near-final PQ1 hardware.
- Nico offered a hardware booth with inspection equipment (e.g., for fault injection testing, voltage glitching) so attendees can verify device integrity.
- Nicola mentioned using Ledger Donjon-style fault injection tools on their boards.
- Freedom Factory also applied to speak at OpenHardware-related sessions.

sections.heading: Optimized MLDSA-44 Verification on EVM
sections.summary: Fireblocks reduced MLDSA-44 on-chain verification cost from 8 million to 1.2 million gas through EVM assembly optimization, costing roughly 22 cents per verification.
sections.body:
- Oren from Fireblocks presented an optimized MLDSA-44 (Dilithium) Solidity verification contract.
- Reduced verification gas cost from ~8 million to 1.2 million gas for a fully FIPS-compliant MLDSA-44 signature (when key is already registered).
  - One-time key registration (expansion and on-chain storage) costs ~4 million gas.
  - Without pre-registration, naive on-chain key expansion costs ~9 million gas.
  - Expanded key is 20 KB; compressed public key is ~2 KB — bandwidth and calldata costs are a consideration for block capacity.
- Key optimization techniques:
  - Avoided EVM's quadratic memory expansion by using small scratch memory instead of expanding everything.
  - Packed 4 elements per 256-bit EVM word for parallel computation.
  - Rewrote critical paths in Yul/EVM assembly.
  - Minimized memory shuffling; directly copied encoded key material from memory instead of decoding.
  - SHAKE-256 gas reduced from ~3 million to ~0.4 million.
- Used Fable AI in auto-research mode for about a week to find optimizations; token cost was not tracked but described as "not cheap" (sponsored by Fireblocks).
- Code ran against the full NIST test suite plus fuzzing and partial formal verification; not yet audited.
- Contract to be published open source imminently.
- Oren estimated no more than ~10% further gas reduction is possible; returns were diminishing.
- At current mainnet gas prices, verification cost is approximately $0.22 (per Simon Masson's calculation).
- Antonio argued this result strengthens the case against adding PQ cryptographic precompiles (e.g., the proposed Dilithium precompile for Hegota or the NTT precompile proposal).
  - The NTT precompile proposal had only reduced MLDSA cost from 8 to 5.7 million gas, less than what pure EVM optimization achieved.
  - Even for threshold/distributed key use cases of lattice-based signatures, precompiles appear unnecessary.
